title: Staking and Liquid Staking (LSTs)
objectives: Trace where Solana staking yield actually comes from
Understand the LST exchange rate that compounds without any claim transaction
Know why an LST can trade below its redemption rate in a panic, and what that trade really is
See what happens to a validator that goes offline

steps.title: Proof of Stake: Where Does Solana Yield Come From?
steps.body:
Every yield has a source, and on Solana that source is the network's own monetary policy plus a slice of transaction-ordering profit. None of it is free money — it is <Term id="staking">staking</Term> rewards the protocol pays for security.

The analogy that sticks: a bank that pays its guards not in cash but in newly printed bank shares. Honest guards keep earning; a guard who lets robbers in gets nothing and is fired. Solana works like that. <Term id="validator">Validators</Term> run servers that order transactions and vote on blocks, locking SOL as a bond to prove they are honest.

Where the yield comes from:

- **Protocol inflation.** The network mints roughly 6% to 7% of total SOL supply each year and hands it to stakers in proportion to their stake weight.
- **MEV tips.** Validators capture fees and ordering value from the transactions they process, and a share flows back to the people staking with them.
- **Commission.** Every validator takes a small cut, typically 0% to 8%, to cover expensive servers and voting costs, then passes the remainder to you.

So the headline rate is gross inflation, and your real return is that number minus the validator's commission. Staking is not lending and not gambling. It is renting your SOL out to secure the chain and getting paid in freshly issued SOL for doing it.

steps.title: Native Staking vs. Liquid Staking Tokens (LST)
steps.body:
Stake SOL natively and the network moves your tokens into a Stake Account and effectively freezes them. Your balance still exists, but the SOL is committed to a <Term id="validator">validator</Term> and cannot be spent or swapped. Want it back? Deactivate the stake and wait through a cooldown of about one epoch — roughly 2 to 3 days.

Think of it as a hotel safe. Very secure, but you cannot buy dinner with the money inside it.

Liquid staking hands you a keycard you can spend while the deposit stays locked:

- You deposit SOL into a pool such as Jito, Marinade, or Sanctum.
- The pool delegates your SOL across many top validators and keeps earning rewards on your behalf.
- In return you receive a yield-bearing receipt token — an LST, like JitoSOL or mSOL.

Now you can do everything locked stake cannot. Provide liquidity on Orca, post the LST as collateral on Kamino, or sell it on Jupiter in seconds. Same underlying stake, same rewards, but the value stays liquid and composable across DeFi. That is the entire meaning of *liquid* in <Term id="liquid_staking">liquid staking</Term>.

steps.title: The Up-Only Exchange Rate Myth vs. Reality
steps.body:
There are two ways staking rewards can reach your wallet, and LSTs use the quieter one. Some tokens are rebasing — your balance simply grows, so 100 tokens quietly becomes 102. Solana LSTs use an appreciating exchange rate instead: your token count never changes, but each token becomes redeemable for more SOL over time.

`1 LST = (1 + accrued yield) SOL`

Watch JitoSOL grow at 7%:

- At launch: 1 JitoSOL = 1.000 SOL
- After one year: 1 JitoSOL = 1.070 SOL
- After two years: 1 JitoSOL = 1.145 SOL — compounding, not a flat 7% each year

That gap between a flat <Term id="apr">APR</Term> and a compounding <Term id="apy">APY</Term> is why long-term staking quotes quote APY: each epoch's rewards are swept into the pool's reserves and earn rewards on top. The ratio `sol_reserves / lst_supply` ticks up automatically. No claim transaction, no daily rebase — just a rate that climbs quietly while you hold.

steps.title: Why Can LSTs 'Depeg' on Secondary Markets?
steps.body:
Here is the distinction that trips people up: an LST has two different prices.

- **Protocol redemption rate.** What the stake pool contract will pay you per LST at epoch boundaries, backed by the SOL sitting in the pool. This is the real value.
- **DEX market price.** What buyers and sellers will trade an LST for right now on an AMM. Supply and demand set this minute to minute.

Picture a gold ring genuinely worth $500, with a frantic seller accepting $475 because they need cash today. The ring never changed — the buyer's urgency did.

During extreme crashes — the FTX collapse in November 2022 is the classic example — leveraged traders holding <Term id="liquid_staking">liquid staking</Term> tokens need cash immediately. They cannot wait two to three days to unstake natively, so they dump millions of dollars of LST straight into AMM pools. That flood crashes the DEX price below the protocol rate and the token appears to depeg.

The opportunity: that discount is payment for patience. A patient arbitrageur buys the LST at, say, 0.95 SOL on the DEX, starts an official unstake, and when the epoch ends redeems each token for the full ~1.00 SOL protocol rate. The spread is the reward for absorbing the seller's time pressure.

steps.title: Under the Hood: Solana Epoch Rewards & Slashing
steps.body:
A Solana epoch is 432,000 slots, roughly 2.5 days. At each boundary the runtime sweeps every stake account and pays inflation rewards based on how diligently its <Term id="validator">validator</Term> voted that epoch.

Reading the reward machine:

- Validators that vote reliably on the right fork receive the full reward for the stake delegated to them. One that misses votes earns less, and one that goes offline earns nothing.
- Unlike Ethereum, Solana does **not** currently slash — burn — a validator's stake automatically for downtime. The punishment is economic instead: poor validators earn zero <Term id="staking">staking</Term> rewards and delegation bots move stake away from them.
- When you hold an LST all of this happens behind the scenes. The pool's SOL reserves grow by the rewards earned, which updates the `sol_reserves / lst_supply` exchange rate.

That is why an LST's value drifts upward without any action from you. Rewards land in the reserves, the denominator stays fixed, so each unit's claim on SOL rises. The <Term id="apr">APR</Term> advertised is really a forecast of how fast that ratio will climb — and because the pool restakes the rewards, it compounds into an <Term id="apy">APY</Term> over time.

questions.prompt: You hold 100 JitoSOL and the official protocol exchange rate is 1 JitoSOL = 1.10 SOL. How much SOL can you redeem by unstaking through the pool?
options: 100 SOL
90 SOL
100 SOL minus a 10% commission penalty
110 SOL
questions.explainRight: The appreciating rate means each token is worth more than one SOL, so 100 × 1.10 = 110 SOL. Your token count never grew — only the value per token did. That is exactly how LSTs deliver auto-compounding rewards.
questions.explainWrong: Multiply, do not subtract. There is no exit penalty in the official pool; the extra 10% is accumulated staking yield baked into the rate, not a fee. The validator's commission is already accounted for before the rate is published.

questions.prompt: Why do many Solana users choose liquid staking (an LST) over native staking?
options: LSTs pay measurably higher inflation rewards than native staking on the same validator
LSTs are the only way to avoid paying any validator commission
An LST stays liquid, so it can be traded or used as collateral while the underlying stake keeps earning, avoiding the multi-day unstaking cooldown
Native staking permanently destroys your SOL, so it can never be recovered
questions.explainRight: The rewards are the same underlying staking yield; the difference is liquidity. An LST lets you trade, lend, or post collateral while your SOL keeps staking, so capital is never idle for the epoch cooldown.
questions.explainWrong: The headline yield is essentially the same — the gain is liquidity. Native staking does not destroy your SOL. An LST wraps the same stake in a transferable receipt so you can keep using the value elsewhere.

questions.prompt: One staking protocol advertises 7% APY while another shows 7% APR. What is the key difference between these two numbers?
options: APY includes the effect of compounding rewards, so the APY figure reflects a higher effective annual return than the same APR
APR is the rate you pay to borrow and APY is the rate you earn, so only one applies to stakers
They are identical, and the second label is just a marketing typo
APY is always exactly double APR because it is computed twice a year
questions.explainRight: APR is the raw rate before compounding; APY folds in the fact that earned rewards are restaked and then earn rewards themselves. Because LST pools auto-restake each epoch, the effective return runs above the flat rate.
questions.explainWrong: Both describe returns here — the difference is compounding. APY is the higher figure and matches what your position actually earns if rewards keep restaking. There is no fixed 2x relationship.

questions.prompt: An LST trades at a 5% discount on an AMM even though the underlying stake is completely safe and the protocol redemption rate is unchanged. What best explains the discount?
options: The validator backing the pool was hacked and its stake was burned
AMMs are required to charge a 5% exit fee on all staking derivatives
Impatient sellers dump LST into AMM pools during a crash because they need liquidity now and refuse to wait 2-3 days through the native unstaking cooldown
The discount is the protocol's inflation tax withheld at each epoch
questions.explainRight: The stake is fine; the sellers are desperate. Crash-era leveraged holders need cash immediately and cannot wait through unbonding, so they sell into AMM pools at whatever price clears. The discount is the price of instant liquidity, not a sign of insolvency.
questions.explainWrong: The gap has nothing to do with a hack, an AMM fee, or inflation. It appears when desperate sellers accept a lower DEX price to get liquidity now rather than wait days to unstake natively.

questions.prompt: An arbitrageur buys JitoSOL on a DEX at 0.95 SOL while the protocol redemption rate is 1.00 SOL, then immediately starts a native unstake. Why is this described as a 'near risk-free' trade?
options: Because AMMs automatically refund the discount to anyone who initiates an unstake
Because the protocol fixes how many SOL are redeemed per token, so the 0.95 to 1.00 spread is locked in once the unstake completes
Because the arbitrageur also shorts SOL, which removes all price exposure from the position
Because staking protocols pay a guaranteed bonus for every native unstake request
questions.explainRight: The arb is not betting on SOL's direction — the protocol guarantees a fixed number of SOL per token at redemption. Buying at 0.95 and later redeeming at 1.00 locks the ~5% spread regardless of where SOL moves in the meantime. The only cost is waiting through the epoch.
questions.explainWrong: The edge comes from a guaranteed redemption quantity, not from refunds, grants, or a hedge. No protocol pays a bonus — the profit is simply the gap between the two prices, and the wait is exactly the liquidity the impatient seller paid to skip.

questions.prompt: A Solana validator goes offline for three consecutive epochs. Based on this lesson, what is the most accurate outcome for the people staking with it?
options: The validator's entire locked stake is slashed and burned, wiping out stakers' principal
The validator earns zero staking rewards for those epochs and delegation bots redirect stake away, but its staked principal is not automatically slashed
Stakers keep earning full rewards because the network guarantees a minimum payout regardless of validator performance
The protocol confiscates the validator's server hardware as compensation to stakers
questions.explainRight: On Solana today, downtime is punished economically rather than by burning stake. An offline validator forfeits its rewards for those epochs and delegation bots move stake to better-behaved validators. Stakers lose the yield they would have earned, not their SOL.
questions.explainWrong: The distinction that matters is lost rewards versus lost principal. Solana does not currently auto-slash for downtime, so stakers are not wiped out — but they earn nothing and the validator bleeds delegations. There is no minimum reward guarantee.

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the difference between an LST's protocol redemption rate and its DEX market price?
options: The two are always equal, which is why arbitrage is unnecessary in liquid staking
The protocol rate is set once at launch and never changes, so the DEX price is the only real measure of value
The DEX price is fixed to the protocol rate by the issuer, so a genuine discount is impossible

The protocol rate is the value backed by on-chain SOL that the pool guarantees to redeem at epoch boundaries, while the DEX price floats with supply and demand and can temporarily sit above or below it
questions.explainRight: The protocol rate is the SOL-backed value the stake pool will honour at an epoch boundary, and it rises with accrued rewards. The DEX price is a live market quote that can trade at a premium or a discount. Arbitrage is the mechanism that pulls the two together.
questions.explainWrong: The protocol rate does change — it climbs with rewards — and the DEX price is not pinned to it. The two diverge whenever liquidity or urgency imbalances the AMM, which is exactly what makes the arbitrage exist.
